newsitem.title: ITALY: New Olivetti head says will sell PCs, other units.
newsitem.headline: New Olivetti head says will sell PCs, other units.

text.p: Italian high-tech group Olivetti's top manager promised on Thursday to quickly sell off a string of businesses, including a loss-making personal computers unit, and to nurse the company back to profit by 1998.

Chief executive officer Roberto Colaninno told financial analysts in Milan he planned to divest Olivetti's ailing PC business and three other units by the end of this year thereby raising some 800 billion lire ($526 million).
It was Colaninno's first presentation to the financial community since his appointment last month to replace Francesco Caio, who was forced out of the company within three months of taking the helm.
Olivetti's future lay in its telecommunications interests, Colaninno said, adding it had "to recover its vocation as an industrial company and make remunerative products".

Investor concerns over the state of the company came to a head when a former director general, Renzo Francesconi, resigned one month ago after casting doubt on the accuracy of the group's first half results. The company's shares plunged as a result.
Colaninno said in addition to the troubled PCs division, Olivetti also planned to sell its Tecnost business which makes automated teller machines for banks and ticketing systems.
Decision Systems International, a company providing maintenance services for mainframe computers, and a venture capital business, Venture Capital USA, would also be sold by the end of 1996.
He said further interests would be sold in 1997, raising the total the company planned to raise from divestments in 1996 and 1997 to beteen one and 1.2 trillion lire.
"In 1997 we plan to divest non-commercial activities," he said without elaborating. "The aim is to bring the company to a position where it is not eating up cash in 1997."
Olivetti also intended to go ahead with a planned flotation of its office equipment subsidiary Lexikon on the New York stock exchange in the course of 1997.

Colaninno said Olivetti aimed to restore its finances through the sale of assets and he ruled out making a rights issue to shore up the balance sheet. "The priority is the company's financial equilibrium," he told a meeting of financial analysts in Milan. "The solution is not through a capital increase, this is a hypothesis which does not arise."
Olivetti's net indebtedness has escalated in recent months, jumping to 2.39 trillion lire at end August from 1.26 trillion at the end of June.
Asked when Olivetti might return to profitability, Colaninno replied: "I have not yet established the plan for 1997 which will be a year of transition...but 1998 will have a positive result."

He also confirmed that Olivetti planned to sell an eight percent stake in Omnitel Sistemi Radiocellulari to Germany's Mannesmann but this would not affect Olivetti's control over the company. Omnitel Sistemi is the vehicle through which Olivetti exercises a controlling interest in mobile phone venture Omnitel Pronto Italia.
Analysts said they were impressed by Colaninno's presentation but added that the credibility of Olivetti, which has not turned a profit since 1990, had been severely strained after years of losses.
"It's very early to judge because they have to deliver on all these promises," said an analyst who has followed the company for a number of years.
Colaninno is scheduled to give another presentation to financial analysts in London on Friday morning.

In a separate development, former Olivetti chief executive Corrado Passera was added to a list of people associated with the company who are being investigated in connection with Olivetti's first half accounts.

Passera resigned suddenly from Olivetti in June. Others under investigation include his successor Caio, honorary chairman Carlo De Benedetti, chairman Antonio Tesone and financial manager Giorgio Airaudo. ($1=1520 Lire)
